title: Grade 4 Multiplication Word Problems: 4 Story Types + Free Quiz
meta_title: Grade 4 Multiplication Word Problems + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Spot the four story types that mean multiply, write the number sentence, and solve grade 4 multiplication word problems, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: The hard part of a Grade 4 multiplication word problem is not the arithmetic — it is knowing it wants you to multiply at all. Here are the four story types that always mean multiply, and how to turn each into a number sentence you can solve.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Here is a Grade 4 problem I have watched trip up bright children more times than I can count: ‘A kirana shop sells eggs in trays of 30. Ravi buys 15 trays for a wedding. How many eggs is that?’ The child can do 30 × 15 on paper once you show them the sum — the trouble is spotting that the story wants multiplication in the first place. That, not the calculation, is the real skill in grade 4 multiplication word problems, and it is the one that gets skipped.

The good news: at Grade 4, almost every multiplication story belongs to one of just four types. Learn to recognise the four, and you can read a problem, know instantly that it means multiply, and write the number sentence before you touch the working. Let me walk through them with the kind of examples your child will actually meet.

The four story types that mean ‘multiply’

Multiplication is not only ‘repeated addition’. That description fits the first type and quietly misleads children on the other three. Here are all four, in the order I teach them.

1. Equal groups

The classic. You have some number of groups, each holding the same amount. ‘A box holds 24 pencils. A school orders 7 boxes.’ Seven groups of 24 means 24 × 7 = 168 pencils. The tell-tale signal is a phrase like ‘each’, ‘every’, or ‘per’ — ‘each box’, ‘every packet’, ‘25 per row’.

2. Arrays and area

Rows and columns. ‘An auditorium has 18 rows of chairs with 22 chairs in each row.’ That is an array, and the total is 18 × 22 = 396 chairs. Anything laid out in a grid — tiles on a floor, plants in a garden, a chessboard of laddoos — is an array problem. Children who have drawn arrays in Grade 3 recognise these fastest.

3. Rate and ‘per’ problems

A rate links two different units. ‘An auto charges ₹12 per kilometre. Meena rides 14 kilometres.’ The cost is 12 × 14 = ₹168. Rate problems hide inside prices (₹ per item), speed (km per hour), and packaging (grams per packet). If you can slip the word ‘per’ into the sentence and it still makes sense, it is very likely a multiply.

4. Comparison — ‘times as many’

This is the one children get wrong, because it looks like it might be addition. ‘Anil has 16 stamps. His grandfather has 8 times as many.’ The grandfather has 16 × 8 = 128, not 16 + 8. The signal words are ‘times as many’, ‘times as much’, ‘twice’, ‘thrice’. Whenever a story compares two amounts using ‘times’, it is multiplication — full stop.

Turning a grade 4 multiplication word problem into a number sentence

Once you have named the type, the number sentence almost writes itself. I have children ask three questions, out loud, before writing anything:

  • What is the size of one group, one row, or one unit? (24 pencils, 22 chairs, ₹12 per km.)
  • How many of them are there? (7 boxes, 18 rows, 14 kilometres.)
  • Am I being asked for the total? If yes, multiply the two numbers.

So ‘24 pencils per box, 7 boxes, find the total’ becomes 24 × 7. Writing the sentence before the working is a small habit with a big payoff — it stops the panicked child who multiplies two numbers just because they appear in the question.

Solving with multi-digit multiplication

Grade 4 is where the numbers grow teeth. A 2-digit × 1-digit sum like 24 × 7 is manageable, but the syllabus pushes into 2-digit × 2-digit — the 30 × 15 from our egg problem, or 24 × 15. Here is the column method for 24 × 15 done properly:

  • Multiply by the ones digit: 24 × 5 = 120.
  • Multiply by the tens digit: 24 × 10 = 240 (write the 0 in the ones place first).
  • Add the two partial products: 120 + 240 = 360.

So Ravi’s 30 trays — sorry, 15 trays of 30 — give 30 × 15 = 450 eggs. The single most common error I see is not the times-table fact; it is forgetting to shift the second row one place to the left. Line the columns up on squared paper and half those mistakes vanish.

When multiplication is only one step

Real problems rarely stop at one operation. ‘A shopkeeper buys 12 cartons of biscuits, each carton holding 24 packets. He sells 250 packets. How many are left?’ Here multiplication is step one — 24 × 12 = 288 packets in total — and subtraction is step two: 288 − 250 = 38 packets left. Grade 4 is full of these two-step stories, and the trick is to solve them one clause at a time rather than hunting for a single sum.

My honest advice: resist the urge to teach ‘keyword tricks’ like ‘total always means add’. They fall apart the moment a problem says ‘total cost’ and means multiply. Naming the story type is slower to learn but never lies.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The eight questions below are all Grade 4 multiplication stories — equal groups, arrays, rates and ‘times as many’ — with a couple of two-step ones mixed in. Let your child read each carefully, name the type, and write the number sentence before choosing an answer. When they are ready for longer graded practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives dozens more, with a full answer key.

faq.q: How do I know when a Grade 4 word problem needs multiplication?
faq.a: Look for one of four story types: equal groups (‘each’, ‘per’), arrays (‘rows and columns’), rates (‘₹ per item’, ‘km per hour’) and comparison (‘times as many’). If the story fits any of these and asks for a total, you multiply.

faq.q: Why do children add instead of multiply on ‘times as many’ problems?
faq.a: The word ‘times’ sits next to two numbers, so it looks like a join. But ‘8 times as many as 16’ means 16 × 8 = 128, not 16 + 8. Teaching ‘times as many always means multiply’ fixes this quickly.

faq.q: What size numbers should a Grade 4 child multiply?
faq.a: Grade 4 covers 2-digit × 1-digit (like 24 × 7) building up to 2-digit × 2-digit (like 24 × 15). The column method with partial products is the reliable way to reach that level.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake in 2-digit multiplication?
faq.a: Forgetting to shift the second row one place to the left. When you multiply by the tens digit, the answer belongs in the tens column, so write a 0 in the ones place first. Squared paper prevents most of these slips.
